title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction: §XXII finishes the change of variables begun in §XXI. Earlier sections derived the equilibrium equations of a perfectly flexible plane thread using intrinsic loads: a tangential force p ds and a normal force q ds per element. Here the applied load per element is instead given in fixed Cartesian components: P ds along XA (the axis direction) and Q ds along MX (the ordinate direction). The angle φ = XMT satisfies sin φ = dx/ds and cos φ = dy/ds. Resolving the load gives the tangential component p = P sin φ + Q cos φ along MT. The normal component along mr is q = Q sin φ − P cos φ. This is just a rotation of the force vector by the tangent angle. Euler then poses Problem I, the catenary: a uniform, perfectly flexible thread hangs from two points under gravity alone. In the solution (§XXIII) the axis AX is vertical and pointing upward, so the ordinate y is horizontal. Only P acts and Q = 0. If a length b of thread weighs B, an arc of length s weighs sB/b and the element weighs B ds/b, which must equal P ds. On the next page Euler sets β = B/b, so p = β sin φ and q = −β cos φ, giving p ds = β dx and q ds = −β dy. The general equations dT = β dx and T dφ = β dy then give T = βx + C. This leads to the standard catenary dy = D dx/√((βx+C)² − D²), with logarithmic construction, and to βs = √((βx+C)² − D²) + E. The page serves to specialise the general flexible-line theory to a classical test case.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page. Euler's own sign conventions are internally consistent: with sin φ = dx/ds and cos φ = dy/ds, the components p = P sin φ + Q cos φ and q = Q sin φ − P cos φ are correct projections onto MT and the chosen normal mr.
Minor: on the next page the transcription has 'ob q=0', which should read 'ob Q=0' (it is Q, the horizontal load, that vanishes).

ideas.what: Resolution of a distributed load given in Cartesian components into tangential and normal components along a plane curve
ideas.modern_name: Rotation of force components into the Frenet (tangent–normal) frame of a string
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard; used by Jakob Bernoulli, Johann Bernoulli, and Euler throughout his flexible-body and mechanics work
ideas.where_published: Euler's Mechanica (E15/E16, 1736), and his various papers on flexible threads and sails

ideas.what: Catenary as an application of the general tangent/normal equilibrium equations dT = −p ds, T dφ = q ds (with Euler's signs)
ideas.modern_name: Catenary via intrinsic string equilibrium equations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Catenary: Leibniz, Huygens and Johann Bernoulli (1691). Intrinsic equations for flexible lines: Jakob Bernoulli and Euler; Truesdell, 'Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies' (1960), discusses E410
ideas.where_published: E410 itself (Novi Comm. Petrop. 15, 1771); also in earlier Euler treatments of the catenary, e.g. the Methodus inveniendi (E65, 1744)

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains a routine resolution of forces and the set-up of the classical catenary problem. Both are well known, credited, and treated in Truesdell's historical study of E410. Nothing unfinished or uncredited appears.
transcription_corrections: Margin note reads 'Tab. VII. Fig. 5.' as transcribed; the plate number in the scan could possibly be read 'VIII', so verify against the plates.
'nostro methodo' is as printed (sic; classical Latin would be 'nostra methodo').
